section.heading: 3.11. Hyperbolic Functions
Hyperbolic Functions and Their Derivatives
section.paragraph: Certain combinations of the exponential functions $$e^{ x}$$ and $$e^{- x}$$ arise so frequently in mathematics and its applications that they deserve to be given special names. In many ways they are analogous to the trigonometric functions, and they have the same relationship to the hyperbola that the trigonometric functions have to the circle. For this reason they are collectively called hyperbolic functions and individually called hyperbolic sine, hyperbolic cosine, and so on.

note.title: Definition of the Hyperbolic Functions
note.heading: Definition of the Hyperbolic Functions
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{ll} {\sinh x = \frac{e^{ x} - e^{- x}}{2}} & { {csch}x = \frac{1}{\sinh x}} \\ {\cosh x = \frac{e^{ x} + e^{- x}}{2}} & { {sech}x = \frac{1}{\cosh x}} \\ {\tanh x = \frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}} & { \coth x = \frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: Some of the mathematical uses of hyperbolic functions will be seen in Chapter 7. Applications to science and engineering occur whenever an entity such as light, velocity, electricity, or radioactivity is gradually absorbed or extinguished because the decay can be represented by hyperbolic functions. The most famous application is the use of hyperbolic cosine to describe the shape of a hanging wire. It can be proved that if a heavy flexible cable (such as an overhead power line) is suspended between two points at the same height, then it takes the shape of a curve with equation $$y = c + a\cosh\left( {x \slash a} \right)$$ called a catenary (see Figure 4). (The Latin word catena means “chain.”)

image.alt: Details An illustration shows two towers superimposed on the x y coordinate plane. One tower is on the negative x axis, the other is on the positive x axis. A U-shaped curve connects the high points of the towers. The lowest point of the U-shaped curve is on the positive y axis.

section.paragraph: Another application of hyperbolic functions occurs in the description of ocean waves: the velocity of a water wave with length $$L$$ moving across a body of water with depth $$d$$ is modeled by the function
$$\upsilon = \sqrt{\frac{gL}{2\pi}\tanh\left( \frac{2\pi d}{L} \right)}$$
where $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity (See Figure 5 and Exercise 57).

image.alt: Details An illustration shows a water wave, resembling a sine curve, with three low points and two high points. A dashed horizontal line is superimposed on the wave such that the low points of the wave lie below the dashed horizontal line, and the high points lie above it. The horizontal distance between the low points of the wave is labeled L. The vertical distance from the dashed horizontal line to the bottom of the sea level is labeled d.

section.paragraph: The hyperbolic functions satisfy a number of identities that are similar to well-known trigonometric identities. We list some of them here and leave most of the proofs to the exercises.

note.title: Hyperbolic Identities
note.heading: Hyperbolic Identities
note.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{ll} {\sinh\left( {- x} \right) = - \sinh x} & {\cosh\left( {- x} \right) = \cosh x} \\ {\cosh^{2}x - \sinh^{2}x = 1} & {1 - \tanh^{2}x = {sech}^{2}x} \\ {\sinh\left( {x + y} \right) = \sinh x\cosh y + \cosh x\sinh y} & \\ {\cosh\left( {x + y} \right) = \cosh x\cosh y + \sinh x\sinh y} & \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: The identity proved in Example 1(a) gives a clue to the reason for the name “hyperbolic” functions:

If $$t$$ is any real number, then the point $$P\left( {\cos t,\sin t} \right)$$ lies on the unit circle $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ because $$\cos^{2}t + \sin^{2}t = 1$$ . In fact, $$t$$ can be interpreted as the radian measure of $$\angle POQ$$ in Figure 6. For this reason the trigonometric functions are sometimes called circular functions.

image.alt: Details A unit circle with center (0, 0) is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. From the origin O, two radii are drawn: one runs horizontally rightward on the positive x axis and intersects the circumference at a labeled point Q, the other slopes upward to the right, and intersects the circumference in the first quadrant at a labeled point P(cos(t), sin(t)). The area of the sector, bounded by the two radii and the circular arc, is shaded.

section.paragraph: Likewise, if $$t$$ is any real number, then the point $$P\left( {\cosh t,\sinh t} \right)$$ lies on the right branch of the hyperbola $$x^{2} - y^{2} = 1$$ because $$\cosh^{2}t - \sinh^{2}t = 1$$ and $$\cosh t \geqslant 1$$ . This time, $$t$$ does not represent the measure of an angle. However, it turns out that $$t$$ represents twice the area of the shaded hyperbolic sector in Figure 7, just as in the trigonometric case $$t$$ represents twice the area of the shaded circular sector in Figure 6.

image.alt: Details The horizontal orientation of the hyperbola x^2 minus y^2 = 1 is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The hyperbola has two branches. The branch of the hyperbola which opens leftward, enters the second quadrant at the top left, goes down and to the right, reaches its vertex on the negative x axis, and then continues to go down and to the left in the third quadrant. The branch which opens rightward, enters the first quadrant at the top right, goes down and to the left through a labeled point P(cos h(t), sin h(t)), reaches its vertex on the positive x axis, and then continues to go down and to the right in the fourth quadrant. From the origin, two segments are drawn: one runs horizontally rightward on the positive x axis and reaches the vertex; the other slopes upward to the right in the first quadrant and reaches the point P(cos h(t), sin h(t)). The area between the two segments bounded by the second part of the hyperbola, in the first quadrant, is shaded.

section.paragraph: The derivatives of the hyperbolic functions are easily computed. For example,
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\sinh x} \right) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{e^{ x} - e^{- x}}{2} \right) = \frac{e^{ x} + e^{- x}}{2} = \cosh x$$

We list the differentiation formulas for the hyperbolic functions as Table 1. The remaining proofs are left as exercises. Note the analogy with the differentiation formulas for trigonometric functions, but note that the signs are different in some cases.

section.heading: Inverse Hyperbolic Functions and Their Derivatives
section.paragraph: You can see from Figures 1 and 3 that sinh and tanh are one-to-one functions and so they have inverse functions denoted by $$\sinh^{- 1}$$ and $$\tanh^{- 1}$$ . Figure 2 shows that cosh is not one-to-one, but if we restrict the domain to the interval $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ , then the function $$y = \cosh x$$ is one-to-one and attains all the values in its range $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ . The inverse hyperbolic cosine function is defined as the inverse of this restricted function.

$$\begin{array}{lll} {y = \sinh^{- 1}x} & \Leftrightarrow & {\sinh y = x} \\ {y = \cosh^{- 1}x} & \Leftrightarrow & {\cosh y = x {and} y \geqslant 0} \\ {y = \tanh^{- 1}x} & \Leftrightarrow & {\tanh y = x} \end{array}$$
The remaining inverse hyperbolic functions are defined similarly (see Exercise 32).
We sketch the graphs of $$\sinh^{- 1}$$ , $$\cosh^{- 1}$$ , and $$\tanh^{- 1}$$ in Figures 8, 9, and 10 by referring to Figures 1, 2, and 3.

section.paragraph: Since the hyperbolic functions are defined in terms of exponential functions, it’s not surprising to learn that the inverse hyperbolic functions can be expressed in terms of logarithms. In particular, we have:
$$\sinh^{- 1}x = \ln\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right)x \in {\mathbb{R}}$$
$$\cosh^{- 1}x = \ln\left( {x + \sqrt{x^{2} - 1}} \right) x \geqslant 1$$
$$\tanh^{- 1}x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left( \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} \right) - 1 < x < 1$$
Formula 3 is proved in Example 3. The proofs of Formulas 4 and 5 are requested in Exercises 30 and 31.

section.paragraph: Notice that the formulas for the derivatives of $$\tanh^{- 1}x$$ and $$\coth^{- 1}x$$ appear to be identical. But the domains of these functions have no numbers in common: $$\tanh^{- 1}x$$ is defined for $$|x| < 1$$ , whereas $$\coth^{- 1}x$$ is defined for $$|x| > 1$$ .

The inverse hyperbolic functions are all differentiable because the hyperbolic functions are differentiable (see Appendix F). The formulas in Table 6 can be proved either by the method for inverse functions or by differentiating Formulas 3, 4, and 5.
